grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: ein Koffer → der Koffer · eine Tür → die Tür · ein Haus → das Haus · Die Tür ist zu. Die Tür ist offen.
grammar.note_en:
German nouns name people and things and begin with capital letters: der Koffer (“the suitcase”), die Tür (“the door”), das Haus (“the house”). Learn each noun together with its article. Der, die and das all mean “the” here. They distinguish three grammatical genders: masculine, feminine and neuter. Gender is a property of the noun; a house is not a male or female person. Our examples are singular: each noun phrase refers to one person or thing. The nominative is the case used here for the subject—the person or thing the sentence says something about. In Der Koffer ist blau (“The suitcase is blue”), der Koffer is the subject. These are not yet all the article forms German uses.

Ein and eine introduce something: Das ist ein Koffer (“That is a suitcase”), Das ist eine Tür (“That is a door”), Das ist ein Haus (“That is a house”). Masculine and neuter nominatives use ein; feminine nominatives use eine. After introducing something, a definite article can point back to it: Ein Mann kommt. Der Mann steht vor der Tür (“A man arrives. The man stands outside the door”). Ein and der are not interchangeable labels for gender: one introduces a suitcase, the other identifies the suitcase under discussion.

Ist means “is.” Its subject here is a single named person, a singular noun phrase or das meaning “this/that.” Das ist Lina means “That is Lina.” In Der Koffer ist blau (“The suitcase is blue”) and Die Tür ist offen (“The door is open”), the describing word comes after ist. Such a describing word is a predicate adjective; blau and offen do not change their endings in these sentences. This does not teach adjective endings before a noun.

A finite verb is a form that agrees with its subject and shows tense; ist is finite here. A statement normally places its finite verb in the second constituent: Der Schlüssel ist im Haus (“The key is inside the house”). A constituent is a sentence unit; der Schlüssel is two words but one unit. A yes/no question starts with the verb: Ist der Schlüssel hier? (“Is the key here?”). A question word comes first in Wo ist der Schlüssel? (“Where is the key?”), Wer ist im Haus? (“Who is inside the house?”) and Was ist nicht offen? (“What is not open?”). Nicht negates a statement: Der Name ist nicht Mira means “The name is not Mira.” Aber means “but”; und means “and.”

Hier (“here”) is the place near the speaker; dort (“there”) points farther away. In the conversation Lina and Mira can each say hier while standing in different places. Follow the speaker and the stated object: they briefly mean different suitcases. Learn vor der Tür (“outside/in front of the door”) and im Haus (“inside the house”) as two complete location expressions. Der inside vor der Tür is not the nominative article for Tür. It is part of a different case pattern, explained later; do not change die Tür into der Tür in other positions by analogy.

The story also gives you reading forms: kommt (“comes/arrives”), geht (“goes”), wartet (“waits”), steht (“stands/is standing”), heißt (“is called”) and öffnet die Tür (“opens the door”). Recognise these whole forms in context; full conjugation comes later. You are not asked to produce them in the answers. All refer here to one person or thing. The grammar tables consolidate forms already present in the story; use them as a reference rather than a memorisation task.
